item.content:encoded:
ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. — Willson Contreras stood at his locker Saturday afternoon and showed reporters the spot where a pitch hit his right hand in Texas on Thursday.
It was on the knuckles between his pinky finger and ring finger, and there was still swelling and a yellow bruise. Contreras could flex his hand but can’t yet grip a bat well enough to hit.
If you didn’t know Contreras was a baseball player, you’d think he was a boxer based on his battered hands.
“When I got hit, I felt my hand going numb. I thought it was bad because that’s a sign of a fracture,” he said. “That’s why I came off the game.”
Contreras is hopeful of getting in a few games before the start of the postseason.
“Hand’s still really sore. Woke up feeling a little better,” he said. “I can squeeze a little better than [Friday], but it’s gonna take a few days.”
The initial X-rays were negative, and any further scans will wait until after the swelling goes down, but Contreras is confident there isn’t a fracture based on his experience.
“I can squeeze a lot better. I’ve had fractures before, and when I have fractures, I couldn’t squeeze,” he said.
Contreras is hoping he can take some swings on Sunday. But because the injury is to his top hand, he has to make sure he can absorb the impact of making contact.
“I’m going to take it day-to-day. Of course I want to come back and play with the guys and be there for them,” he said. “It’s a part of baseball.”
Contreras said he might try using a guard over his batting glove to protect his hand.
The Sox play the Rays on Sunday afternoon and are off on Monday. Contreras could possibly return on Tuesday against the Guardians.
“I’m going to do everything in my power to get back on the field before the playoffs,” he said.
Contreras has been hit 24 times this season, tied for third-most in the majors, and 47 times over last two seasons. It’s largely because he stands close to the plate. But Contreras suggested on Thursday that Sox pitchers should retaliate on his behalf.
“I see, and completely feel and understand Willson’s frustration,” interim manager Chad Tracy said. “He’s been hit close to 50 times the last couple of years so he’s frustrated. Whether he’s referring to the umpires doing something or the pitchers, it’s irrelevant.”
Tracy acknowledged that Contreras crowds the plate. “But there’s a lot of guys that are close to the plate that don’t get hit as much as he does,” he said.
Rafaela progressing
Ceddanne Rafaela, who has been on the injured list since Sept. 3 with a strained right quadriceps, worked out at Worcester on Saturday and faced live pitching for the first time since the injury.
“I felt comfortable,” he said. “My body is rested, and I feel ready to go.”
The last hurdle is to sprint at 100 percent effort, something he will try on Sunday. Rafaela hopes to play against the Guardians on Tuesday.
Crochet could face hitters
Tracy said the goal set for Garrett Crochet would be to face hitters early in the week. That would likely be at Fenway Park before a game. Whether one such session would be enough to merit inclusion on the postseason roster isn’t certain. “Hard to say. I know that’s not a great answer, but it just really is,” Tracy said. … Righthanded reliever Tyron Guerrero could be activated off the injured list as soon as Sunday. He has been out since Sept. 1 with a sore shoulder.
Globe staff writer Alex Speier contributed to this report from Worcester.

RedSoxRoundtable's Zach Coe discusses the latest on a number of key injured Red Sox players. Be sure to join our FREE community over on RedSoxRoundtable.com!
Ahead of the Boston Red Sox series opener at Tropicana Field against the Tampa Bay Rays on Friday, interim manager Chad Tracy met with the media and provided updates on a number of injured Red Sox players.
Here's what you need to know:
All eyes were on the All-Star first baseman after Thursday night's win over the Texas Rangers. Contreras exited the game in the eighth inning after being hit by a pitch on the right-hand. According to MassLive.com's Chris Cotillo, Contreras told reporters after the game that the injury "felt" like a fracture. While initial X-Rays were negative, as the team learned with infielder Curtis Mead, that doesn't mean Contreras was completely out of the woods yet. According to MLB.com's Ian Browne, the team is waiting for swelling in the 34-year-old's hand to subside before testing his grip strength to determine if additional testing is needed.
Contreras is out of the lineup for Friday's series opener.
Crochet threw a 30-pitch up-and-down bullpen session on Tuesday back at Fenway Park, representing the most labor-intensive of the four throwing sessions the 27-year-old has done since restarting a throwing progression Aug. 3. According to WEEI's Rob Bradford, Crochet will throw another side session on Saturday as he continues to work his way back from left shoulder inflammation that has kept him out since April 29.
After turning to Garrett Whitlock to lock down Thursday's win, Tracy told reporters, including Cotillo, that Chapman was unavailable with LAT tightness. According to Bradford, Chapman said the injury popped up ahead of Tuesday's series opener in Texas and that he wasn't concerned about the injury, saying the latest he would return to the mound would be during the team's upcoming home stand, beginning on Tuesday night, if he doesn't make an appearance in Tampa.
Tyron Guerrero
After landing on the injured list on Sept. 1 with right shoulder inflammation. The 35-year-old flamethrower was expected to be activated when he was first eligible, ahead of Wednesday's game in Texas. However, after experiencing lower back tightness, the team delayed his activation. According to Bradford, Guerrero "felt fine" after throwing 20 pitches off the mound on Friday afternoon. However, it still remains unclear when he may be activated.
The 32-year-old outfielder landed on the injured list last Friday with a "right foot ligament injury" after getting it caught in the grates along the center field wall in the Sept. 8 loss to the Los Angeles Angels. As Bradford noted, White has been diagnosed with a ligament tear, likely ending his season.
White's injury seems to open the door for Spring Training standout Braiden Ward to join the Red Sox as a fourth outfielder/pinch runner in the playoffs.
Up next for the Sox
The Red Sox will look to carry the momentum from Thursday's come-from-behind win into the final road series of the year against the Rays. Ranger Suarez (7-4, 3.33 ERA) will get the start for the Red Sox opposite Ian Seymour (9-6, 4.27 ERA) for the Rays. First pitch from Tropicana Field is set for 7:10 p.m. ET.

Boston Red Sox fans were already going through it on Thursday night after Willson Contreras left the series finale against the Texas Rangers early after being hit by a pitch on the hand. Seeing Garrett Whitlock emerge from the bullpen to close a 4-3 game in the ninth inning only made fears worse.
Whitlock is no slouch, as Red Sox fans know, and he got through the ninth frame unscathed, but fans expect to see Aroldis Chapman in moments like that. After the game, Boston announced that Chapman was unavailable due to a lat issue.
Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy said in his September 17 postgame presser that Chapman has been dealing with lat tightness for a couple of days but that he's been improving lately. Boston has classified him as day-to-day and it will routinely check on his recovery progress to gauge his availability.
The best news from Tracy on Chapman is that the team will not place him on the injured list. The Sox's bullpen has been one of their deadliest weapons all season and Chapman with his 1.95 ERA, 34 saves, blistering velocity and unmatched consistency at 38 years old has been a huge part of that success.
Aroldis Chapman injury news is a blow the Red Sox's bullpen can't afford as the playoffs near
Still, having Chapman at anything less than 100 percent is dangerous this late in the season with the playoffs on the horizon. In a tight game, one slip-up in the ninth inning could lead to disaster.
The rest of the Red Sox's bullpen is hardly in its best shape. Justin Slaten's season ended following continued flexor issues and Tyron Guerrero is still on the IL bouncing back from shoulder inflammation. Erik Miller is also dealing with a mechanical issue that has severely impacted his command over his last two outings.
If Chapman's injury is as mild as Tracy is letting on and he doesn't need an IL stint, Boston might be able to avoid disaster. But it also needs Chapman's help to clinch its playoff spot in the first place. The offense is struggling to get out to enough of a lead that it doesn't need Chapman to hold a slim margin in the late innings, but that won't fly in the postseason, especially with an injured closer.
At least the Red Sox expect some relief reinforcements in the coming days. Tanner Houck and Garrett Crochet are working towards returns from long-term injuries in a relief role and they could take some pressure off the 'pen, but neither could fill Chapman's role.

ARLINGTON, Texas — Nearly three months after Caleb Durbin first dislocated his left pinkie and more than a month after he reinjured it, the third baseman’s digit remains locked nearly at a right angle.
“It doesn’t quite straighten or bend all the way,” Durbin acknowledged.
Durbin received X-rays after his initial injury against the Rockies on June 24 and the reinjury against the White Sox on Aug. 6. In both instances, there was no fracture and he was told playing was simply a matter of pain tolerance.
And so, there was little question about how he’d proceed. He didn’t seek more information.
“There really is kind of a joint understanding [with the team] that we’ll get it looked at at the end of the season if we have to, because [whatever the diagnosis is], it’s not going to impact my decision to play at all,” he said.
Still, Durbin recognizes fingers shouldn’t look like they could be used to mount a shelf. Might he require offseason surgery?
“I don’t know yet. We’ll find out,” he said. “I hope there’s something we can do about it. But we’ll get there when the time comes.”
For now, Durbin remains a lineup constant. Thursday’s contest against the Rangers marked his 145th game of the season. He continues to deliver Gold Glove-caliber defense (his six outs above average lead AL third basemen) while also pushing the envelope on the field with high-IQ plays, most recently advancing from first to third on an infield single on Wednesday.
“He plays the game that way,” said Sox interim manager Chad Tracy. “It’s what he does.”
Still, it seems the injury is impacting him at the plate. He’s hitting .211/.400/.316 in September — showing fight in his at-bats (thus his standout on-base percentage), but rarely driving the ball. His whiff rate (10 percent of swings) is the lowest for any month this year, but he’s rarely been able to drive the ball. His 48 percent ground ball rate is his highest in any month since May.
But to Durbin, the question of whether or how the injury might be affecting him is secondary. His primary concern is simply whether he is positioned to contribute in any way.
“The pain’s gone down drastically since it happened the second time,” Durbin shrugged. “It’s functional.”
Updates on injured trio
Garrett Crochet, who last threw off a mound on Tuesday, worked out at Polar Park in Worcester on Thursday and will continue to throw on flat ground on Friday before the team decides whether to introduce any higher-intensity activities over the weekend.
Tracy said there’s been no discussion about the lefthander pitching in a rehab game for the WooSox this weekend. He didn’t rule out the possibility Crochet could soon face hitters in a live batting practice session, but made clear that there is no known schedule involving the 27-year-old.
“It all depends on how he’s feeling. … He’s been down so long,” said Tracy. “It is day to day. [Friday he’ll] throw, see how he feels, and then determine what the weekend holds.”
Righthander Tyron Guerrero, whose return from shoulder inflammation was delayed slightly by lower back cramps, had a high-intensity throwing session on flat ground. He’s expected to throw off a mound Friday when the Sox open a three-game series at Tampa Bay, a potential prelude to activation later in the weekend. “The shoulder feels great, the arm feels great,” said Guerrero.
Ceddanne Rafaela is increasing (right quad strain) is increasing his agility work but, at this point, there’s “no discernible timeline yet on game action,” according to Tracy. It hasn’t been determined if Rafaela will join the Sox in Tampa.
Oviedo in Worcester
Righthander Johan Oviedo (right elbow strain), pitching in an official game for the first time since March 30, struck out four batters while sitting at 96 miles per hour and touching 99 with his four-seamer in 2⅓ innings in a rehab appearance for the WooSox. He threw 20 of 30 pitches for strikes … Ranger Suarez will start for the Sox on Friday against the Rays, but the Sox have yet to decide who will start the other two games of the series. Payton Tolle, Patrick Sandoval, and Brayan Bello are all considerations … The Red Sox will send two scouts to New York for next week’s four-game Yankees-Rays series, the start of the team’s in-person advance scouting efforts for the postseason.

RedSoxRoundtable's Zach Coe discusses the potential relievers who could step up and fill the void left behind by Justin Slaten after it was revealed the right-hander was unlikely to return from the injured list in 2026. Be sure to join our FREE community over on RedSoxRoundtable.com!
After an incredible July that saw the Boston Red Sox go 21-4, ultimately saving their season and propelling them into postseason position, the team has given key contributors time on the injured list to address lingering injuries. Among the players placed on the IL was right-handed reliever Justin Slaten, who was dealing with right elbow soreness.
After initially expecting to miss the minimum of 15 days or somewhere close to it, the 29-year-old continued to experience soreness as he began throwing progressions, leading the team to shut him down each time. On Tuesday, interim manager Chad Tracy announced that Slaten received a PRP injection to treat "degenerative changes in his flexor mass," ending his season.
With Slaten set to miss the remainder of the year, the pressure is on these pitchers to help bridge the gap between the starter and All-Star closer Aroldis Chapman:
Tyron Guerrero
Guerrero was expected to be activated off the injured list ahead of Wednesday night's loss to the Texas Rangers, but tightness in his lower back led the team to delay his activation. Still, though, upon his activation, Guerrero will become one of the primary seventh-inning options for Tracy to turn to.
The 35-year-old flamethrower has been an incredible find for Chief Baseball Officer Craig Breslow, posting a 3.26 ERA in 38.2 innings in 2026. However, he hit a rough patch before landing on the IL, allowing eight earned runs in his last 13.2 innings. Boston will need him to return to the pitcher he was for the first 38.2 innings of his season, when he posted a 2.16 ERA.
After not allowing a single earned run in his first 10 appearances after being dealt to Boston at the trade deadline, the 28-year-old lefty has struggled in his last six outings, allowing five earned runs, including three in a blow-up appearance in Wednesday's loss.
Miller told reporters after the loss that he was working through a mechanical issue that led to the struggles. However, he is the primary left-handed high-leverage arm before Chapman, so the team will need him to get those issues squared away ahead of what's likely to be a Wild Card-round matchup against a New York Yankees lineup that's lefty-heavy.
No single pitcher has stepped up more for the Red Sox as they shuffled Garrett Whitlock, Slaten, and Guerrero on the injured list than Weissert. After a brief demotion to Triple-A Worcester on Aug. 7, Weissert returned to the big leagues on Aug. 13, taking Whitlock's spot on the active roster, and has been lights out ever since. In 10.2 innings since being recalled, the 31-year-old right-hander has allowed only two earned runs on 12 hits, striking out 14 and walking only four.
Weissert figures to be the leader in the clubhouse to take over Slaten's role in the bullpen.
A trio of injured options
The Red Sox have several pitchers looking to return from the injured list before the end of the regular season who could factor into the team's playoff push, including 2025 Cy Young Award runner-up Garrett Crochet, 2024 All-Star Tanner Houck, and Johan Oviedo.
Crochet
The 27-year-old ace has thrown four bullpen sessions since restarting a throwing progression on Aug. 3, with his most recent outing, a 30-pitch up-and-down session on the Fenway Park mound, coming on Tuesday afternoon. While Crochet, if healthy enough to appear in games, will almost certainly be on the postseason roster, he is expected to make multi-inning appearances rather than one-inning spurts like Slaten had been used, making him a valuable weapon but an imperfect replacement.
Houck
The now-30-year-old right-hander is attempting to return to the Boston staff in a "Swiss Army knife" role after undergoing Tommy John surgery in August 2025. Houck has already made three rehab appearances with both Double-A Portland and Triple-A Worcester, allowing two earned runs on one hit, walking four, and striking out seven in 4.2 innings. He is expected to return to Worcester on Saturday for a 40-50 pitch outing before potentially rejoining the Red Sox.
Though what exactly Houck can contribute after being out of major league action since May 2025 remains to be seen.
Oviedo
A bit of a forgotten man in the 2026 Red Sox season is the 28-year-old right-hander, who made only one appearance before landing on the injured list on April 3 with right elbow inflammation. Oviedo will make his first rehab appearance Thursday night with Worcester before deciding on next steps; at this point, the risk likely outweighs the reward of making the postseason roster.
Tracy, Breslow, and the rest of Boston's decision makers will have 10 games to make their final decisions on how exactly the postseason roster will look, and who will replace Slaten's high-leverage innings.
Up next for the Sox
The Red Sox will look to avoid the sweep at the hands of the Texas Rangers in Thursday's series finale from Globe Life Field. Sonny Gray (17-5, 2.76 ERA) gets the start for Boston opposite Tyler Alexander (5-2, 3.38 ERA) for Texas. First pitch is set for 8:05 p.m. ET.

item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox are still sitting comfortably in the second Wild Card spot, but there are several issues they must resolve before they start thinking about playoff baseball.
Boston is a mediocre 11-11 over its last 22 games. While that's been good enough to sustain its playoff position, its play hasn't exactly inspired optimism for a deep postseason run.
Most of the Red Sox' problems can be linked to their underperforming lineup. Key hitters like Roman Anthony, Willson Contreras, Adley Rutschman and Wilyer Abreu have been concerningly inconsistent.
A deeper dive into the numbers suggests the struggling Sox will have their work cut out for them in their presumed Wild Card Series rematch at Yankee Stadium. Here are the club's five biggest areas of concern with 10 games remaining:
Roman Anthony is ice-cold
The Red Sox need Roman Anthony to be one of their best offensive players to have any chance of a deep postseason run. If the former No. 1 prospect continues to play the way he has for most of September, that will be problematic.
Anthony is hitting just .149 (7-for-47) with one home run and a .428 OPS over his last 11 games. He has struck out 18 times in 51 plate appearances.
The 22-year-old's struggles beg the question: should he still be the leadoff hitter in the postseason? Interim manager Chad Tracy will have no choice but to reevaluate Anthony's spot in the lineup if his woes continue. The problem with that is there aren't any exciting alternatives. The leadoff spot has been a glaring issue all season long, regardless of who has been thrust into the role.
Struggling against high velocity
The Red Sox offense has been inconsistent no matter who's on the mound, but it has mostly struggled against pitchers with high velo. Here's how some of Boston's regulars have fared this season against pitches greater than or equal to 97 mph:
- Wilyer Abreu: .170 BA, .623 OPS (237 pitches)
- Jarren Duran: .065 BA, .300 OPS (203 pitches)
- Willson Contreras: .170 BA, .512 OPS (166 pitches)
- Ceddanne Rafaela: .205 BA, .449 OPS (157 pitches)
- Roman Anthony: .091 BA, .440 OPS (58 pitches)
- Adley Rutschman: .077 BA, .451 OPS (57 pitches)
The Red Sox' top performer against high velocity (97 mph and above) has been Caleb Durbin (.364 BA, .912 OPS, 161 pitches).
Being so vulnerable against high velocity will especially be a problem for Boston in its expected Wild Card Series matchup against the New York Yankees. Cy Young frontrunner and likely Game 1 starter Cam Schlittler averages 98 mph with his four-seam fastball, which he uses 44.5 percent of the time. Gerrit Cole averages 96.9 mph with his four-seam, using it 49.3 percent of the time.
Leaving runners stranded
Boston has been below average all season at capitalizing on runners in scoring position. It currently ranks 17th in batting average (.250) and 21st in OPS (.731) with RISP. They're hitting just .212 in such situations through 14 games so far in September.
The Yankees' elite pitching staff probably won't provide the Red Sox with many scoring opportunities in their short series, so it's imperative that they come through when given the chance. Lately, Boston hasn't had anyone in its lineup to feel confident about when they step to the plate with runners on.
Role players regressing
As great as guys like Willson Contreras, Caleb Durbin, and Wilyer Abreu were throughout the Red Sox' incredible midseason turnaround, it was the role players who powered their surge. Mickey Gasper, Jahmai Jones, Nick Sogard, Anthony Seigler, and Andruw Monasterio were instrumental in resurrecting Boston's season.
Gasper has cooled off, though no one expected him to sustain his Barry Bonds-like run. Jahmai Jones is 4 for his last 22 (.182) with nine strikeouts, suddenly making him a playoff roster cut candidate. Sogard is still hitting, but his .758 OPS so far in September suggests regression to the mean. Seigler is hurt. Monasterio posted a .578 OPS in August and is 0-for-11 so far in September, putting him on the playoff roster bubble.
That group deserves immense credit for getting the Red Sox here, but it cannot be counted on to propel the club through the postseason.
Erik Miller experiencing command issues
Boston's bullpen is arguably its biggest strength heading into the postseason. The back end with Garrett Whitlock, Tyron Guerrero, and Aroldis Chapman is elite.
We would've included trade deadline addition Erik Miller in that group last month, when he allowed only one earned run with 20 strikeouts and just three walks across his first 11 appearances with the Red Sox. His performance so far this month, however, has been alarming.
Miller, acquired from the San Francisco Giants in the Marcelo Mayer trade, has allowed four earned runs with six walks and six strikeouts through five appearances (4.1 IP) in September. His command struggles were a question mark upon his joining the club, and it appears that issue has reemerged with less than two weeks until the playoffs.
After Wednesday's poor outing against the Texas Rangers (2 H, 3 ER, 1 BB), Miller attributed his recent struggles to his mechanics. The Red Sox will hope that whatever the problem is, it's a quick fix, because Miller will be counted on to be their most reliable left-handed reliever not named Aroldis Chapman.

When Erik Miller on September 16 took the mound in front of the Texas Rangers, it didn't take long for things to go awry. Miller's command has never been perfect, but something was definitely off in Arlington, Texas.
It took only three pitches for the big lefty to plunk Corey Seager, and he walked Jake Burger two batters later. On his lone pitch to Brandon Nimmo, the former New York Met knocked a game-changing RBI double to center field, and things crumbled from there.
Ezequiel Duran's two-RBI single, which gave the Rangers a three-run lead, was the last at-bat of the inning before Miller was spared by Adley Rutschman catching Duran stealing. The outing was Miller's worst since he joined the Boston Red Sox at the trade deadline — he allowed three runs on two hits, a walk and a hit batter with one strikeout.
The outing against the Rangers was the second one in as many games that has given Miller trouble. On September 13 against the Kansas City Royals, Miller lasted just a third of an inning after conceding two walks and a fielder's choice. Garrett Whitlock entered after him and gave up a single, but the Royals' lone run of the game was charged to Miller.
Red Sox need Erik Miller to right recent command issues as soon as possible to be right for postseason
After his appearance in Texas, Miller made a concerning statement about his recent struggles. It could be a disastrous sign for Boston's October bullpen.
"Kinda working through some stuff right now," Miller said. "There's some stuff I'm trying to clean up a little bit on the mechanical side. I mean, at some point throughout the year, stuff crops up. I had been doing really well and there are some bad habits I'm kinda falling back into so, yeah, just gotta work through it, gotta get back to what I was doing and go from there."
Miller has been one of Boston's biggest relief weapons since the trade deadline. The Red Sox need him in his best shape all the more with Tyron Guerrero on the injured list and after the announcement that Justin Slaten's season has ended.
Before his shaky command popped up, Miller had done a solid job at limiting free passes, one of the major concerns from his tenure with the Giants. Over his 12 outings in August (including one with the Giants) Miller allowed three walks and a hit batter (0.943 WHIP). Through five outings in September, he's up to six walks and a hit batter (2.077 WHIP). The combination of fatigue and decreased command will make for a brutal outcome for Boston.
Thankfully, the Red Sox are expecting some relief reinforcements for the playoff run. Tanner Houck and Garrett Crochet are working toward returns in long relief. But having them plus prime Miller would be the best outcome.
The Red Sox must work more closely with Miller to address his mechanical issue, whatever it is. Over his last two outings, he's served up damaging pitches or free passes, and that won't get Boston far in October, especially given the fatigue its rotation has been showing.

Good morning! Last night, Jake Bennett was unable to hold the Rangers in check during the team's 7-3 loss in Texas. Some of his numbers look good (seven strikeouts against just one walk), but he also surrendered eight hits in just 4.2 innings, which did in his evening.
With just ten games left in the season, the question now becomes how should the Sox use Bennett going forward? With some combination of Sonny Gray, Payton Tolle and Ranger Suarez likely to get lined up in a best of three Wild Card Series, do you just hold Bennett on the sidelines and hope he gets to come back into the fold as a fourth starter in the ALDS or even ALCS? Or do you start transitioning him to some sort of relief role?
It's a bit of an awkward moment for Bennett. He's been getting knocked around during his last two outings while Suarez is seemingly getting locked in. It almost certainly cuts him out of the Wild Card rotation, and if the Sox get some combination of Garrett Crochet, Tanner Houck and Tyron Guerrero back to add to Aroldis Chapman, Garrett Whitlock and Erik Miller in the bullpen, Bennett largely gets squeezed out of relevance.
So how do you want him used? Do those six shutout innings Bennett threw against the Yankees back on August 29th make you want the Sox to find a role for him if they play New York? Do you think he's just a young pitcher who looks out of gas and want to hide him until the team needs a fourth starter?
Use this space to talk about Bennett and the rest of the difficult upcoming pitching staff decisions, and, as always, be good to one another.

RedSoxRoundtable's Zach Coe disscusses the reemergence of Greg Weissert as a reliable relief option for the Red Sox bullpen.Be sure to join our FREE community over on RedSoxRoundtable.com!
After a historic July that saw the Boston Red Sox use high-leverage arms on a near-nightly basis, one of baseball's best bullpens became injury-ravaged, losing Garrett Whitlock, Tyron Guerrero, and Justin Slaten to fatigue-related injuries. The losses of Whitlock, Slaten, and Guerrero forced interim manager Chad Tracy to turn to other relievers in high-leverage spots. Among those arms is right-hander Greg Weissert, who, after a brief trip to Triple-A Worcester, has come up huge for the bullpen.
In his first 48 appearances of the season, Weissert posted a 3.97 ERA in 45.1 innings pitched. The 31-year-old right-hander struggled in particular when taking over in situations with men already on base, allowing 13 of 29 inherited runners to score, which, at the time, was the third-most among all relievers.
After needing 34 pitches to get through an inning in Boston's 13-inning marathon win over the Chicago White Sox on Aug. 6, Weissert fell victim to the numbers game, getting optioned to Triple-A Worcester on Aug. 7 in favor of a fresher arm. However, it wound up being just a six-day trip as he was recalled on Aug. 13 when the team placed Whitlock on the IL.
In 12 appearances since being recalled, Weissert has more than made up for the losses of Whitlock, who returned on Aug. 29, Guerrero, who is slated to return ahead of Wednesday's game in Texas and Slaten. He's allowed only two earned runs on 11 hits, striking out 13 and walking only four in 10.2 innings of work. Most importantly, Weissert has performed much better when entering 'dirty' innings, allowing only one of seven inherited runners to score.
Despite Whitlock's return and Guerrero's imminent return, Weissert's reemergence as a reliable option will help in the final 11 games of the regular season and the postseason run, as Tracy announced Tuesday that Slaten will not return in 2026 after undergoing a PRP injection in his right elbow to treat degenerative changes in his flexor mass.
Up next for the Sox
After falling 4-2 in Tuesday night's series opener against the Texas Rangers, the Red Sox will look to even up the series in game two of three from Globe Life Field on Wednesday night. Rookie left-hander Jake Bennett (9-7, 3.69 ERA) will get the start for Boston opposite fellow southpaw MacKenzie Gore (8-11, 4.62 ERA) for Texas. First pitch is set for 8:05 p.m. ET.

item.content:encoded:
Over the last few weeks, or so, it has seemed like pretty much every injury update for the Boston Red Sox has been positive.
Garrett Crochet has been throwing, Tanner Houck has been on a rehab assignment and even Curtis Mead has been playing catch, among others. While this is the case, the Red Sox gave a negative update on Wednesday. Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy shared that reliever Justin Slaten is dealing with "degenerative changes in the flexor mass" and is likely done for the 2026 season.
"Slaten, we got ... he went and saw [Dr. Keith Meister] with our medical staff today and there's some degenerative changes in the flexor mass," Tracy said. "So he's going to be down. He's going to get a PRP injection and it's likely going to end his season. So, that's substantially different news, as far as these guys."
Bad News For Boston
This is a brutal blow for Slaten, and the Red Sox's bullpen in general. Slaten is one of the club's key high-leverage guys, but Boston hasn't had him on the mound since Aug. 12. He was initially placed on the Injured List due to right elbow inflammation. He actually started throwing, but he had to be shut down when the same "symptoms" that landed him on the Injured List popped up again.
Slaten had a 4.60 ERA in 36 appearances, but this doesn't tell the full story about why he's a big loss for Boston. In his final 17 appearances of the season, he had a 2.45 ERA and a 19-to-3 strikeout-to-walk ratio in 14 2/3 innings pitched. The first half of the season wasn't great for him, but he had turned things around and looked like the guy Boston hoped it would have out of the bullpen.
The Red Sox have just 11 games left in the 2026 regular season. Losing Slaten hurts Boston's playoff chances. On the bright side, the Red Sox's bullpen could still get better with Houck on a minor league rehab assignment and Garrett Crochet throwing as well. With Slaten likely out for the season, that's one less change Boston will have to make when building the playoff roster. Tyron Guerrero, Crochet, and Houck are all inching their way back. Boston will have to clear three spots to get these guys on the roster. That could be bad news for guys like Greg Weissert, Wyatt Olds, and Raymond Burgos, among others.
With Slaten likely not coming back, it's one less decision for Boston to make. Of course, it would be better if he were returning, but that isn't the case right now. Unfortunately, Red Sox fans have seemingly seen the last of Slaten for the 2026 season.

ARLINGTON, Texas — For the Red Sox, the vision of contention in 2026 seemed straightforward.
The team’s championship window had been pried open by the presence of a pair of cornerstones, with Garrett Crochet anchoring the rotation and Roman Anthony representing a lineup anchor not only for this year but several seasons to come.
But while the Sox are amid a magic-number countdown to a playoff berth, they’ve done so without Anthony and Crochet for most of the year. Their season has been saved in no small part by players who have emerged from obscurity to play critical roles — with essential contributions coming from Andruw Monasterio, Anthony Seigler, Mickey Gasper, Tsung-Che Cheng, Jahmai Jones, Tyron Guerrero, and more.
“I don’t think anybody had that on the drawing board,” said interim manager Chad Tracy with a chuckle. “They were asked to play a lot, and they produced. And if they didn’t, we were in trouble. It’s a huge piece of the 2026 season, no question.”
Of course, while no one expected the outsized impact of players who began the year as big league backups or in Triple-A, the Sox also took considerable pains to build organizational depth through a variety of transactions.
Whether it was an expanded version of the trade that brought Caleb Durbin from Milwaukee to include Monasterio and Seigler, or waiver claims of Cheng and Gasper, or a minor league deal for Guerrero, the season has been a case study in the notion that perceived little moves can have a huge impact.
“Every move and every decision matters,” said assistant general manager Mike Groopman, who oversees the team’s acquisitions group. “The big ones, whether it’s a larger free agent deal, [or] a larger, more high-profile trade, is naturally going to get a lot of attention.
“I don’t think this is unique to the Red Sox. There are 29 other teams that try to and do a very good job about caring about the ‘little’ things. But I think what we really try to reinforce is … that year over year, around the game, you see things that seem ‘little’ that end up being really impactful and big. [Deals that] seemed like small moves at the outset end up having a much, much larger impact commensurate with what would have been perceived at the time as a ‘larger’ move.”
Players who evolve from theoretical depth to become big league contributors excite numerous corners of an organization. The primary credit for those contributions, of course, belongs with a player, but they still often represent the combined efforts of personnel in scouting who identify the player’s potential contributions, player development personnel who help the player build on preexisting strengths and abilities in the minors, and big league staffers who help the players to perform at the game’s highest level.
Take Guerrero. After brief stints in the big leagues in 2018 and 2019, he’d become a journeyman, shuffling between organizations — and countries — but unable to forge a way back to the big leagues despite elite velocity.
But the Sox — who’d been interested in signing Guerrero before he pitched in the NPB in Japan in 2025 — remained intrigued, thanks in part to strong scouting recommendations from Kento Matsumoto in Japan and Manny Nanita in the Dominican Winter League. After they signed Guerrero to a minor league deal in the offseason, player development officials worked with him on some minor grip changes that unlocked significantly improved command with a sinker that regularly reached triple digits.
Guerrero’s dominance this year in Triple-A (0.92 ERA) essentially forced the Sox to call him up, and the 35-year-old emerged as a late-innings force from late June to late August (before shoulder fatigue led to a bad outing followed by a trip to the injured list), posting a 2.13 ERA over a 23-appearance stretch.
Again, the lion’s share of the credit goes to Guerrero for the work he did to fight his way back to the big leagues. But his emergence embodies the sort of under-the-radar acquisition that helped save the Sox’ season.
“The connection and integration between acquisition and development is really important,” said Groopman. “Guerrero and our [player development] group put a lot of time into [those changes] in the spring and the early season, to get him to a point where he was able to lock in some of these changes and unlock what was super obvious arm talent into something that was translating more consistently onto the major league mound.”
Of course, talent alone doesn’t dictate success once a depth player gets to the big leagues. They must also have the opportunity to contribute — and, in many cases, the freedom to fail while getting their bearings.
Tracy, who spent time with nearly all of this year’s depth contributors in Triple-A at the beginning of the year, has been mindful of creating an environment in which call-ups can contribute.
“I’m in the same boat [as them]. I want the freedom to go manage the game [as a first-time big league manager],” said Tracy. “I need to manage a game and feel like if I do something that doesn’t go right, it’s not the end of the world. If I feel that way, then I want the player to feel like, ‘Hey, if you go out there and play second base today and you make an error, move on to the next play.’
“If the culture becomes, ‘If I make a mistake, then all of a sudden I clam up and I get really tight,’ we’re going to have a problem. So you look at them and say, ‘You’re here for a reason: To go play your game. Don’t worry about making a mistake. Move on to the next pitch, next play.’ And they did that, and they were awesome.”

BOSTON, MASSACHUSETTS – APRIL 08: Garrett Crochet #35 of the Boston Red Sox pitches against the Toronto Blue Jays during the first inning at Fenway Park on April 08, 2025 in Boston, Massachusetts.
Photo by Brian Fluharty/Getty Images
Chad Tracy and the Red Sox know some reinforcements on the mound are coming.
And speaking ahead of Tuesday's loss to the Rangers, Tracy provided the masses with a mixed bag sort of update on those rehabbing arms trying to work their way back to Boston in time for the final push of the regular season and the playoffs.
Beginning with Garrett Crochet, Boston's ace who has been sidelined since late April, things continue to trend in the right direction, according to Tracy.
"Crochet threw today [and] that went well," Tracy said. "Everything went well. We’ll wait and see on the next steps, [but] that was the most volume he’s had, so we’ll see over the next couple of days how he feels and then we’ll go from there.”
Crochet and the Red Sox have outright said that any return to action this season would by all means have to come in a reliever role. Crochet, meanwhile, has even suggested that he could make his return to the roster in the postseason.
Elsewhere on the rehab front, Tanner Houck took his best step yet in what's been an improbable run back into the picture as a legitimate option for the Red Sox.
On the hill for the Woo Sox in what was his third rehab outing (but first in Triple A), Houck allowed one walk and struck out three batters in one inning out of the bullpen. Houck is now up to seven strikeouts and has surrendered just one hit (but four walks) over 4.2 innings of work through three games between Portland and Worcester.
The hard-throwing Tyron Guerrero, meanwhile, is eligible to return from the injured list on Wednesday. Guerrero has been on the injured list since Sept. 1 with right shoulder inflammation, and could be a hugely important piece of the puzzle for Boston down the stretch given his dominant stretches earlier in the year.
But Tracy's seemingly endless parade of updates also came with some bad news, as he revealed that the club will be without Justin Slaten for the rest of the season.
Justin Slaten #63 of the Boston Red Sox pitches against the Detroit Tigers at Comerica Park.
"There was some degenerative changes in the flexor mass, so he's going to be [shut] down," Tracy said of Slaten, who met with Dr. Keith Meister, and his status moving forward. "He's going to get a PRP injection and likely going to end his season."
Slaten, who has not pitched since has not pitched since the club's Aug. 12 loss to Toronto, had recently started throwing from 90 feet before the shutdown. Slaten had really turned it on over his last 14 appearances prior to landing on the shelf, too, with 14 strikeouts and a 2.19 ERA in 12.1 innings of work before his season ended.
Fresh off a 4-2 loss to the Rangers on Tuesday but firmly in control of the second wild card in the American League, the Red Sox have another 11 games to get Crochet, Houck, Guerrero, and whoever else up to speed before the postseason begins.

The 2026 season has been, for the most part, an injury-plagued loss for Crochet, who made his first six starts before getting shut down with left shoulder inflammation that regressed when he made his first attempted comeback in late May.
But the beauty of all this is that Crochet can wash away the sour taste of missing most of the season by getting back as a reliever in time for the most important games.
After that setback at the end of May, it took Crochet three months just to be cleared to throw off the mound again.
Now that he’s been able to do so three times, and is scheduled for a fourth bullpen session at Fenway Park on Tuesday, there is legitimate hope he can be on the roster when the Red Sox open their postseason on Sept. 29 -- likely at Yankee Stadium.
This time, assuming he makes it back, Crochet will be cast in a much different role, but one that can still be impactful.
Figuring you have questions about how and when Crochet fits in, here are some answers.
Can Crochet make it back before the regular season ends?
It’s not impossible. His next key step after graduating from bullpen sessions will be to face hitters. That could happen as soon as this weekend, depending on what the club decides after Tuesday’s session.
Ideally, when it comes to Crochet’s situation, the Triple-A season would go a little longer. But, alas, it ends on Sunday.
It seems more likely Crochet will throw live batting practice and/or some type of simulated game rather than getting into a Minor League game, perhaps doing so multiple times.
Would this leave time for one tune-up before the regular season ends on Sept. 27? Perhaps, but not necessarily.
Would Crochet be thrown right into the fire of the playoffs?
What if there isn’t time for Crochet to pitch in any type of game setting before the Wild Card Series starts? Would the Red Sox still put him on the roster?
Well, if he’s throwing up to his capabilities, the answer is absolutely yes.
“It's Garrett Crochet,” said Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy. “If Garrett Crochet looks like Garrett Crochet and he's healthy and able to go out there and pitch, and it looks like him? Yeah, that helps any team.”
What would Boston’s bullpen cast look like with Crochet in the mix?
In a word, dominant. Through their first 150 games of the season entering Tuesday, Boston’s bullpen has a 3.11 ERA, best in the Majors. That’s without Crochet.
Now, add Crochet and possibly 2024 Tanner Houck, who is on a Minor League rehab assignment in his return from Tommy John surgery, and Tracy’s relief crew could have a succession of pitchers with nasty stuff.
At 38 years old, lefty Aroldis Chapman continues to be a force. He has one of the best eighth-inning setup men in the game in front of him in righty Garrett Whitlock. Tyron Guerrero, the righty with triple-digit heat, is due back in the next couple of days after missing the last couple of weeks with right shoulder inflammation. Power lefty Erik Miller has been tremendous since he was acquired at the Aug. 3 Trade Deadline.
Brayan Bello, who hasn’t had much success has a starter this season but has been largely stellar in relief, is another weapon. Add Crochet and Houck to those five pitchers and the Sox would have bullpen depth that would be the envy of most teams.
How would the Sox use Crochet?
The beauty of Crochet is that he could work out of a hybrid role, meaning he could be available for whichever part of the game Tracy needs him most.
Keep in mind that Crochet was a relief pitcher not just in college at Tennessee, but also for the White Sox before being converted to a starting role in ‘24. He has experience working in the early, middle and late part of games.
Thinking outside the box, the Sox could even deploy Crochet as an opener if the occasion called for it, given his experience starting games.
“He'd have plenty of comfort opening if you wanted to go that route," Tracy said. "He pitched out of the 'pen. So if you need him to come in the middle innings of a game, a two-inning pocket, I'm sure he'd have comfort doing that, too."

ARLINGTON, Texas — Among a series of minor injury updates offered by Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy on Tuesday came some finality on one key reliever. Righty Justin Slaten, after further assessment by a renowned orthopedist in the Dallas area, won’t return to the Red Sox this year.
Slaten visited Dr. Keith Meister on Monday’s off day and testing on his injured elbow revealed “degenerative changes in the flexor mass,” according to Tracy. Slaten is set for a platelet-rich plasma (PRP) injection that is all but certain to rule out his return in 2026.
“It’s a big loss,” Tracy said, “at least now, with the finality of knowing we can’t have him back.”
Slaten was placed on the injured list with elbow inflammation in mid-August and dealt with recurring discomfort as he tried to resume throwing. As of the weekend, he was completely shut down from his progression. Now, he will receive the injection and rest in hopes of getting the issue fixed for 2027.
“Probably just means a chronic thing over time, but I’m speculating there,” Tracy said. “I just know that the conservative course of action is PRP, then he’s gonna rehab and go from there. Because of that, it’s probably going to cost him the rest of the season.”
Slaten appeared in 36 games for the Red Sox this year, posting a 4.60 ERA as a mid-relief option ahead of setup man Garrett Whitlock and closer Aroldis Chapman. For the third straight season, injuries were a big part of Slaten’s season. In 2024, he missed about six weeks due to elbow inflammation in July and August. Last season, he was out from June 1 to August 28 with a balky shoulder. This year, he suffered an oblique strain in early April and missed 31 games, then hit the IL again for the final six weeks.
Mead takes step forward
For the first time since having his left wrist broken by a wayward pitch in West Sacramento on July 27, Curtis Mead will do some offensive work in Boston on Wednesday. According to Tracy, Mead — who is out of a cast and has been doing defensive and baserunning drills for weeks — will hit lightly off a tee as he begins his swing progression.
“Mead will begin, tomorrow, introducing tee work,” Tracy said. “Obviously, we’ve talked a lot about the defensive stuff, being able to catch throws and he’s been doing that. Tomorrow, he’ll start doing some tee work with a light bat and then just kinda progress from there.”
With just 12 games left in the regular season, Mead is in a race against the clock to be fully ready for game action, a reality he acknowledged just last week. But it’s still notable that he’s ready to start taking swings in anticipation for potentially returning during the postseason if the Red Sox make a run.
Crochet throws again at Fenway
Left-hander Garrett Crochet took another small step toward a late-season return Tuesday, throwing a two-inning “up-and-down” bullpen (that includes a break simulating a between-inning breather) at Fenway Park. That session came four days after a one-inning high-intensity bullpen on the same mound.
“That went well,” said Tracy. “Everything went well.”
The next step for Crochet might be facing hitters in a live batting practice/simulated game setting but it’s very unlikely he’ll be ready to pitch in a rehab game before Triple-A Worcester’s season ends Sunday. A more likely scenario involves him getting into a simulated game or two and then making a relief appearance late in next week’s final homestand of the year.
“We’ll wait and see on the next steps,” Tracy said. “That was the most volume he’s had, so we’ll see how he feels and go from there.”
Guerrero close to return, Kelly has setback
Right-hander Tyron Guerrero, out since September 1 with shoulder inflammation, is with the Red Sox in Arlington and is expected to be activated before Wednesday’s game. Lefty Raymond Burgos and righty Wyatt Olds are the two leading candidates to be sent down as Guerrero takes a roster spot.
“We’ll see how everything goes with that today,” Tracy said.
The return of Guerrero will give the Red Sox another high-octane option at the end of a bullpen that also includes lefty Erik Miller, Whitlock and Chapman (and won’t have Slaten for the rest of the year).
One reliever who won’t contribute the rest of the way is righty Zack Kelly, who has been out since early July with a stress reaction in the olecranon (bone at the tip of the elbow). Kelly had been throwing live BP sessions in Fort Myers and was close to a rehab outing but had a setback last week and will undergo updated imaging this week.
Rafaela progressing
Center fielder Ceddanne Rafaela (right quad strain) has said his goal is to rejoin the Red Sox for this weekend’s series against the Rays and that is still in play. He’s back in Boston and going through strength tests on his leg while ramping up his running program.
“Started to increase running volume today,” Tracy said. “Nothing new to report there. He’ll continue to do that over the next 2-3 days and we’ll see where he’s at.”
The Red Sox could be careful with Rafaela and welcome him back early next week when the Guardians are at Fenway Park.
Houck, Oviedo on track for rehab outings
Right-hander Tanner Houck is pitching for the WooSox at Polar Park on Tuesday as planned. His outing was planned as a shorter relief outing (he entered in the seventh, following six strong innings for starter Jedixson Paez) and he’s expected to make another appearance over the weekend in a longer stint on the mound.
Right-hander Johan Oviedo is still on track to make a rehab start in Worcester on Thursday.

ARLINGTON -- Right-handed reliever Justin Slaten’s season is over, Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy announced ahead of Boston’s three-game series opener against the Rangers at Globe Life Field on Tuesday night.
According to Tracy, Slaten met with Dr. Keith Meister, an orthopedist in the Dallas area, and an evaluation revealed “degenerative changes in his flexor mass” in his right elbow.
“Probably just means a chronic thing over time, but I’m speculating there,” Tracy said. “I just know that the conservative course of action is [a platelet-rich plasma injection]. He’s going to rehab and go from there, but because of that, it’s going to probably cost him the season.”
“As we sit here right now, we were operating and moving forward, planning on having to operate without him,” Tracy said. “This maybe adds some finality to the fact that, ‘OK, now the chances of getting him back are slim.’”
The 29-year-old Slaten posted a 4.60 ERA with 39 strikeouts across 31 1/3 innings over 36 appearances for Boston.
“It’s a big loss,” Tracy said. “At least now the finality of knowing we can’t have him back. But you guys have seen the way he can come in and pitch in those big-moment cleanup innings, to get you out of the sixth, seventh inning. We’ve seen him do that, so he’s an important arm. But we have to deal with it and move on.”
Slaten and Garrett Whitlock served as the Sox’s top right-handed setup men when both went down last month. Whitlock returned from the IL on Aug. 29.
When Slaten and Whitlock first went down, Tracy believed he had enough arms to navigate the bullpen. That depth, however, continues to be tested.
Right-hander Tyron Guerrero, who landed on the IL on Sept. 1 with right shoulder inflammation, was expected to be activated Wednesday but experienced muscle cramping in his lower back Tuesday, delaying his return. According to Tracy, the team does not know when Guerrero will be activated.

ARLINGTON, Texas — Reliever Justin Slaten’s season is all but over after the discovery of a “degenerative” arm issue, Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy said Tuesday before a 4-2 loss to the Rangers.
Before the series opener against the Rangers, Slaten went with team medical staff to visit Keith Meister, a highly regarded orthopedic and sports medicine surgeon based in Arlington.
Meister diagnosed the reliever, who had been out with what the club called right elbow inflammation, with a more serious problem.
“There’s some degenerative changes in the flexor mass,” Tracy said. “So that’s substantially different news.”
The flexor is in the forearm and connects to the elbow. Slaten will receive an injection of platelet-rich plasma, which is supposed to stimulate healing. Tracy called it “the conservative course of action.”
Already, with Slaten’s pain lingering well beyond what the Red Sox figured would be a brief shutdown period when he went on the injured list on Aug. 16, he was trending toward not having time to return this season.
“This maybe adds some finality to the fact,” Tracy said. “We were already operating that way, but you still held out hope. ‘Hey, if it can turn the corner and [with] what he’s able to do out of that bullpen. . . . So yeah, it’s a big loss — at least now, the finality of knowing we can’t have it back.”
For Slaten, who turned 29 on Tuesday, it is another in a string of injuries that have limited his impact. Since reaching the majors in 2024, he has missed time because of elbow, shoulder, and oblique issues.
This year, the righthander had a 4.60 ERA overall and a 2.84 ERA in the two months before getting hurt.
The Red Sox’ top setup options for lefthanded closer Aroldis Chapman remain righthander Garrett Whitlock, lefthander Erik Miller, and righthander Tyron Guerrero. They expect Guerrero back from the IL as soon as Wednesday.
“[Slaten is] an important arm,” Tracy said, “but we have to deal with it and move on.”
Crochet builds up workload
Back at Fenway Park, Garrett Crochet on endured his heaviest workload yet in his bid to return for the playoffs, a 30-pitch bullpen session across two simulated innings.
“Everything went well,” Tracy said. “That was the most volume he’s had, so we’ll see over the next couple of days how he feels and go from there.”
Among other rehabbing pitchers: Tanner Houck made his third rehab appearance and first for Triple-A Worcester, striking out three of four batters (and walking the other). He threw 22 pitches but only 11 strikes.
The Sox’ plan calls for Houck to pitch for Worcester again late this week, throwing 50 or more pitches in a much longer relief appearance. For playoff purposes, they are keeping their options open, experimenting with Houck in short and long relief.
Progress for Mead
Seven weeks after fracturing his left wrist in his first game with the Red Sox, Curtis Mead is starting a hitting progression.
The infielder is due to begin “tee work” with an “underloaded,” lighter-than-normal bat on Wednesday, Tracy said. An ability to swing comfortably has held back Mead, who for weeks has been throwing/playing catch (including recently actually catching the ball thrown back to him).
Also in a race against the calendar, Mead appears unlikely to return this year unless the Red Sox play deep into the postseason
The running man
Ceddanne Rafaela (right quad strain) has “started to increase running volume” and will continue to do so the next several days, Tracy said. The center fielder has said he hopes to return this weekend when the Red Sox visit the Rays . . . Tracy and his staff gathered for a group dinner Monday, their first time doing so since Kansas City in mid-May. “So to be able to get all of us together and have a meal, it was a nice off day,” he said. Who paid? “The Red Sox.”

We've reached the "wake me up for the playoffs" portion of the Boston Red Sox season.
The Red Sox have 12 games remaining on their 2026 regular-season schedule. As of Monday, they sit comfortably in the second American League Wild Card spot with a six-game lead. They're 4.5 games behind the New York Yankees in the Wild Card standings, so barring a shocking development, they'll visit the New York Yankees in the Wild Card Series for the second consecutive year.
Which 26 players will the Red Sox bring with them to the Bronx? Who's on the chopping block? Here's our 26-man playoff roster projection with 15 days until Game 1:
MORE RED SOX
Catcher (2): Adley Rutschman, Connor Wong
Cuts: None
The Red Sox could theoretically cut Wong since he'd barely see the field with Rutschman healthy. If Rutschman went down in that scenario, Mickey Gasper could go behind the plate... but that wouldn't be pretty.
Here's the problem with that approach: If Rutschman gets hurt and the Red Sox add a replacement catcher mid-series, Rutschman would be ineligible for the next playoff round. So if he got hurt in the Wild Card Series, he'd be ineligible for the ALDS and eligible to return in the ALCS.
Putting Wong on the playoff roster ensures that if Rutschman goes down, they won't need to add a mid-series replacement with Wong and Gasper already on board. And while Wong isn't exactly Pudge Rodriguez defensively, he's better than Gasper behind the dish.
Infield (7): Willson Contreras, Trevor Story, Caleb Durbin, Isiah Kiner-Falefa, Nick Sogard, Mickey Gasper, Andruw Monasterio
Cuts: Curtis Mead (IL), Anthony Seigler (IL)
Even with Wong on the roster, Gasper's incredible offensive upside shown in August earns him a roster spot as a bench bat. Monasterio is on the bubble, but recent injuries may have cleared his path to a bench role.
It doesn't look like Mead (wrist) will be healthy in time for the start of the postseason.
Outfield (5): Jarren Duran, Wilyer Abreu, Ceddanne Rafaela, Roman Anthony, Jahmai Jones
Cuts: Eli White (IL), Masataka Yoshida (IL), Nate Eaton
The big question mark here is White's health, as the speedster was recently placed on the 10-day injured list with a foot ligament injury. He'll play a key bench role if healthy, but if he isn't, Jones or Eaton are the top candidates for that fifth outfield spot. We're leaning Jones because of his ability to mash left-handers.
Yoshida (hamstring) probably isn't coming back this year.
Starting rotation (3): Sonny Gray, Payton Tolle, Ranger Suarez
Cuts: Patrick Sandoval
Sandoval just hasn't been reliable, so he draws the short straw. Jake Bennett and the returning Garrett Crochet move to the bullpen -- assuming Crochet is healthy enough to give one or two quality innings in relief.
Bullpen (9): Garrett Crochet, Jake Bennett, Brayan Bello, Greg Weissert, Wyatt Olds, Erik Miller, Tyron Guerrero, Garrett Whitlock, Aroldis Chapman
Cuts: Justin Slaten (IL), Tanner Houck (IL), Johan Oviedo (IL), Alec Gamboa, Jovani Moran, Raymond Burgos
If Slaten's elbow is healthy, he's in, but it doesn't currently look like it will be since he was recently shut down from throwing.
Crochet is trending toward being ready just in time for October. So is Houck, but he hasn't pitched in a big-league game since May 2025, and he hasn't looked sharp in his rehab outings. While his upside is intriguing, we'd leave him off the initial playoff roster.
Brayan Bello makes the cut as a bulk arm after excelling in that role throughout the second half.

item.content:encoded:
Willson Contreras is back with the Red Sox, activated Sunday from the injured list for their finale against the Royals. He collected two hits and a walk in the 4-1 win.
The Red Sox didn’t need to think hard about how to open a spot on the active roster: infielder Anthony Seigler went on the injured list with a right wrist issue.
“We talked a lot about as guys were getting healthy, the conversation was like, ‘What are you going to do?’” interim manager Chad Tracy said. “Stuff’s going to happen, which it always does.”
Contreras missed a dozen games because of a left hamstring strain.
After playing through the leg problem for about a month, Contreras asked the front office to let him more thoroughly rest, figuring a September timeout would serve him well down the stretch and into the playoffs.
On his first day back, he tested it plenty — hustling to first base and advancing to second on an error, moving from first to third on a single.
“I ran a lot today on the field, and my hammy feels pretty good,” Contreras said. “I won’t lie: If I wasn’t feeling really good in [Double-A] Portland, I wasn’t going to play tonight.”
Tracy said: “The point of [going on the IL] was to get [the hamstring] to a point where he felt confident in it, where he can go out and play and not have to worry. And at least like to think we’ve got to that point, which is good.”
In a two-game tuneup with Double-A Portland, Contreras went 2 for 7 with three strikeouts and no walks.
His appearance Saturday yielded a strange episode in the fourth inning. After a ball moved the count to 1-and-1, he called timeout, seemingly to get pine tar. Plate umpire Daniel Bytheway called him back to the plate.
Contreras then all but stopped participating in the plate appearance, leaving the bat on his shoulders for the next four pitches. He struck out looking.
On his way back to the dugout, drawing boos from the Portland crowd, Contreras tossed his bat back toward the plate.
“I didn’t even know until somebody showed it to me this [Sunday] morning,” Tracy said before the game. “I haven’t even seen him and asked him that yet. I think that’s something to do with pine tar.”
Contreras said later Sunday: “I don’t know. You can go ask the umpire. His name is Gary. Thank you.”
The Red Sox didn’t have a diagnosis on Seigler, who hurt himself on a seemingly random swing Saturday, but intended to send him for tests in the coming days.
As the rotation turns
The Red Sox will keep their starting pitchers in line against the Rangers: Patrick Sandoval on Tuesday, Jake Bennett on Wednesday, Sonny Gray on Thursday. Brayan Bello is bumped back to the bullpen following a one-start cameo.
Rehab roundup
The Red Sox will bring Tyron Guerrero (right shoulder inflammation) to Texas and activate him during the Rangers series. They haven’t decided which day. He is eligible to return Wednesday.
Ceddanne Rafaela (right quad strain) told NESN he is planning to return for the Rays series next weekend.
“We’ll call that a goal. It’s not a guarantee,” Tracy said. “It really is dependent on strength numbers in the quad and making sure that’s appropriate, and then he gets through all the sprint volume stuff first, and then we’ll see where he’s at.”
The Sox will leave it up to Rafaela, Tracy added, whether he wants to go on a rehab assignment before returning. Triple-A Worcester is the last affiliate still in season.
Justin Slaten (right elbow inflammation) still has not resumed throwing.
Guest of honor
Beverly native Beckett Connolly, a 10-year-old liver cancer survivor and transplant recipient, threw out a ceremonial first pitch — to hefty applause from the Fenway Park crowd.
